STRATEGIC PLAN CRITICAL SUCCESS FACTORS

 Engaged and Connected Residents
 Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
 Safe Community
 Attractive, Complementary Business District
 Beautiful, Preserved, Single-Family Neighborhoods

BACKGROUND

The Code Enforcement Division is part of the Community Development Department. The
Division is staffed with a Code Enforcement Manager, a full-time Code Enforcement Officer
(Vacant), and a part-time Code Enforcement Officer. On certain occasions, the Community
Development Director will step in to fill some of the duties and responsibilities. The two full
time officers work a standard schedule of 7:00 am to 5:00 pm, although there are some occasions
when they have started their duties before 7:00 am and stayed later past 5:00 pm. The part-time
officer works on a variety of schedules depending on the need. In some cases, this officer works
on Saturdays or Sundays, early morning or into the evening hours.

The Division’s caseload is managed through the help of the GoGov software and mobile
application, which allows the officers the ability to stay organized and efficient. While conducting
their field observations, the Code Enforcement staff utilize the mobile application to help create
cases. The Division exercises its duties by ensuring that the policies and objectives of the Code
Enforcement Policies and Procedures Manual are followed (see attached).

DISCUSSION

During the past several weeks, the Division began to gain some momentum into its re-envisioning.
The re-envisioning includes a significant amount of time on messaging, education, video messaging,
cooperatives with the local groups such as Neighborhood Watch, and creates a system that

 fosters consistency and streamlines compliance with Code violations. To ensure the success of
the new programs listed below, staff and the City must maintain consistency with the
enforcement of the Codes. Although some of these goals have already begun, the very recent
loss of the full time officer has slowed down our momentum.

Despite some of the latest obstacles, the Division is pleased to share with the Council our new
approach towards meeting our goals. The following list will showcase our new efforts as we
move forward with our re-envisioning:

Draft Code Enforcement Policies and Procedure Manual

The attached Draft Code Enforcement Policies and Procedural Manual is a work in progress, and
will provide direction to the Code Officers for many situations including rights of access,
notification procedures, and case management. The most critical part of this manual is the
direction provided with respect towards gaining compliance on a Code violation. It is the
intention of the manual (when completed) to direct the Division to seek compliance within a
certain period, refer matters to the City Prosecutor or to initiate a citation and fine. The goal is
to gain compliance within a short period and to prevent long-term conditions. Staff intends to
have such document reviewed by the City Prosecutor’s office.

External Cooperation

The Division has already begun the relationship-building process with our local Neighborhood
Watch groups. This includes being part of their agendas and discussing with the group the issues
they are seeing in their neighborhoods. The initial goal is to create the relationship and building
the trust of these groups.

Internal Cooperation

The Division has teamed up with various Departments to help with our Code Enforcement
efforts. The Division has met with the Police and Fire Departments to illustrate their role with
Code Enforcement. The goal is to utilize their individual subject matter expertise towards gaining
compliance. Specifically, the Police Department will continue to be our “after hours” staff. The
Police Department will respond and monitor conditions in the City that are violations and report
back to the Division. Such reports will be used to cite the property owner or violator. In
addition, the Division will provide the Watch Commander with the updated list of Tree Permits
issued. This will help the officers as they respond to calls on these matters. The Department
will also assist the Division on locating vacant homes.

In a similar way, the Fire Department will monitor and enforce conditions that pose a fire danger
such as accumulation of debris on structures or on property. The Fire Department will provide
the Code Enforcement Division with the list of properties surveyed that warrant further Code
Enforcement action. The Department will also share with the Division any concerns or violations
upon completion of their annual business inspections.

 Parks and Public Works will continue to manage Lacy Park and the rules associated with the use
of the park. Public Works staff report unsightly conditions related to parkways. Public Works
staff will be encouraged to use the mobile application to report such conditions.

Messaging

The Division will create video messaging and flyers that will help inform and educate the public.
Such information will also be a part of a social media campaign. Staff has already initiated a new
form of correspondence that will help resolve certain matters, such as vacant homes and property
maintenance issues. Specifically, staff has developed a system of surveying the City to locate
vacant homes. When one is found, staff provides the property owner or tenant a letter that
either instructs the occupant to register the home or to remedy any conditions that may be
considered a nuisance.

The Division will create internal messaging for staff that includes summaries of various Codes.
Staff has already prepared such documents for the Vacant Homes Ordinance and Tree
Preservation Ordinance. The goal with this is to help staff outside the Community Development
Department read and understand the Codes in the most simplistic manner.

Public Education

The Division will provide quarterly reports to the City Council on high priority cases and tree
preservation cases. The report will provide a list of high profile cases, updates, and a monthly
“Did you know” message. The Division will also conduct Town Hall Meetings, provide an
Electronic Newsletter, Web Site / Public Education Blog, Commercial / YouTube Channel, and
partner with the San Marino Tribune.

Lastly, the Code Enforcement Division will begin producing regular reports similar to that of the
Police and Fire Departments.

Internal Improvements

To increase our efficiency throughout the City, the Division will be divided into three segments:
East, West and Commercial. Each Code Enforcement Officer will be assigned a segment of the
City to patrol and to manage. The part-time Code Enforcement Officer will be tasked with
managing the early morning hours, after hours and the Commercial area.

The Division will continue to look for Code amendments that will help streamline the process.
The initial goal is to amend the public nuisance laws.

Lastly, the Code Enforcement Division will work with the City Prosecutor’s office and the Police
Department to upgrade our current citation booklet.

 1.0  POLICY DESCRIPTION: OVERVIEW
Purpose:
The purpose of this document is to provide a general overview of the Code Enforcement Division
(Division) within the City of San Marino Planning and Building Department (Department) and the Policies
and Procedures which apply to the Division’s efforts to obtain correction of Code violations. These
services may be supplemented from time to time by the San Marino Police Department.
Overall Philosophy:
This Code Enforcement Policy Manual (CCPM) shall serve as a tool for Code Enforcement Officers in
performing their normal duties related to the goal of obtaining compliance. Additionally, the CCPM
provides guidance to general Departments staff regarding the processing of Code violation cases.
The Code Enforcement Division shall use various techniques to assure compliance with State and local
laws relating to building and zoning requirements, health and safety concerns, property maintenance
standards, and other land use laws and regulations. Its goal is to obtain voluntary compliance from citizens.
Each case may be unique and a “one size fits all” solution doesn’t always work.
Several studies have shown that a good compliance program promotes increased land values, safer
neighborhoods, and pride in ownership. Education of the public regarding applicable laws can be an
effective tool in obtaining immediate compliance, and a long-range solution to ongoing nuisances. Efficient
Code Enforcement is best accomplished by direct communication with members of the community
through a variety of methods. These include reaching out via social media (such as Facebook, Next Door,
and the City Website), mass mailings, and face-to-face discussions with property owners.
Code Enforcement staff shall maintain ethical standards and strive to be firm, fair, and friendly. The
California Association of Code Enforcement Officers defines a Code Enforcement Officer’s goal as one
that serves the community to safeguard lives and property and to respect the Constitutional rights of all
of the members of the community. Code Enforcement Officers strive to achieve a number of objectives.
They work for the common goals of their profession and employer. They conduct themselves as a model
for the community and are accountable and accept professional and personal responsibility. They make
decisions free from prejudice, honor the spirit and letter of the law, and safeguard public confidence by
conducting themselves in a manner that maintains public trust.
The City is committed to maintaining the quality of life in San Marino through obtaining compliance in
enforcing regulations and codes. The Code Enforcement Division shall uniformly and fairly enforce codes
and regulations and shall assign high priority to the abatement of violations that may constitute potential
threats to public health or safety or that may cause significant environmental damage. The CCPM
supplements the adopted San Marino Code.
1.1  Identifying and Prioritizing Code Cases
Purpose:
To provide overall guidelines for prioritizing code cases. The number of violations and the time it takes
to achieve compliance requires staff to make efficient use of limited time and resources. The most efficient
method is to obtain voluntary compliance from those property/business owners and residents who are
found to be in violation of City Codes and State law. Those cases where reasonable progress towards
abatement of identified violations are not feasible shall be referred to the City Prosecutor for legal

 enforcement action(s). In all cases, the Department seeks to avoid Code Enforcement actions that result
in the permanent loss of dwelling units except in cases where a unit was constructed in violation of the
applicable zoning ordinance in place at the time, or where a unit cannot be feasibly rehabilitated to meet
health and safety requirements.
Policy and Procedures:
The Department prioritizes the identification and abatement of Code violations affecting the health and
safety of San Marino residents, employees, and visitors. The Department also prioritizes the abatement of
violations that cause or have the potential to cause environmental harm. Nuisances and other violations
that do not have an immediate potential for harm to people and/or the environment will be a lower
priority. The Department relies on citizen complaints to help identify violations requiring the attention of
Code Enforcement Officers. The Department also identifies potential violations through regular reviews
and inspections conducted pursuant to City Code and/or conditions of approval, as well as independent
investigations of violations associated with short-term rental housing, business license matters, and vacant
homes. In addition, staff may become aware of violations through the direct observation of activities being
conducted without the benefit of permits (or outside the scope of approved permits).
1.2  Chain of Command
Purpose:
To provide clear expectations to Code Enforcement Officers with respect to reporting relationships.
Policy and Procedures:
Every member of the Code Enforcement Division shall follow the established chain of command.
Currently, the chain of command structure begins with the Director, followed successively by the Code
Enforcement Manager, and staff. When it becomes necessary to contact someone in management,
employees will start with their immediate supervisor. If the supervisor is not available, then the Director
will be contacted.
1.3  Training
Purpose:
To offer proper techniques for dealing with the public in an effort to reach compliance.
Policy and Procedures:
The Code Enforcement Division is a customer-service oriented team, whose purpose is to fulfill the
community’s need for Code Enforcement. A professional appearance and demeanor produce both respect
and support from the community and co-workers. Part of being a professional Code Enforcement Officer
is the ability to handle any situation with understanding, care and concern. City of San Marino Code
Enforcement Officers are encouraged to continue to obtain training and education in an effort to improve
the process of reaching compliance. Certification and training sessions are available through the California
Association of Code Enforcement Officers.

 2.0  CASE MANAGEMENT
Purpose:
To ensure quality service, standardize information and facilitate the preservation of accurate records for
all compliance activities; and to continue operation of a system of Code Enforcement that is both effective
and fair.
Policy and Procedures:
Procedures will be established to provide for consistent collection and factual analysis of information
relating to investigations. Detailed records will be maintained and organized for use by the Division, City
Prosecutor and Courts. The following is a guideline to assist all staff in the complaint handling process.
Changes may occur based on individual cases and circumstances, as reasonably determined by the Code
Enforcement Manager. The reason for any change or expedited process shall be documented and
described in the file.
2.1.  Performance Measures
Purpose:
To have a uniform timeframe in which Code Enforcement complaints are investigated.
Policy and Procedures:
In order to measure efficiency, the Department has developed performance measures based upon the
percentage of cases resolved (applications submitted/reviewed/permit issued), and how much time it takes
a Enforcement Officer to perform an Initial Response from the date the complaint is logged. For the Initial
Response indicator, cases are prioritized in the following manner:
Priority 1 – Safety related Complaint (such as building without a permit, unsafe structure, and sub-standard
conditions) with a goal of 5 Working Days for initial response. (NOTE: Various deadlines and times for
completion of tasks as called for in this Manual are stated in terms of “Working Days.” Weekends, City
holidays as well as days when the office is closed for regular business due to a declared or posted
emergency do not constitute working days.” That definition shall be applied in this Manual.)
Priority 2 - Non-Safety related Complaint (Zoning, other) with a goal of 15 Working Days for initial
response. Currently, the Department will create reports from the GoGov App and Accela case
management system. These reports will be used to measure performance and to provide data that can be
used to evaluate and improve the program.
Note: Violators who show no attempt to remedy the violation or provide no progress shall not be given
additional time to correct the matter. Violations that include unresponsive parties shall be referred to
the City Prosecutor, be issued a citation with fine or addressed via public nuisance after the deadline has
passed. Progress towards compliance shall be shown through physical change or via documentation.
Anecdotal responses from the violator shall not be construed as progress towards compliance.
2.2  Records Organization and Electronic File Naming
Purpose:
To have a standardized method for organizing the code enforcement case files in the computer.

 Policy and Procedures:
Currently many files are organized first by address, then by name, then by violation abbreviation. This
method shall continue. A list of abbreviations shall be used. Paper files are currently created based upon
a recognized method for all files in Department. This method shall continue to be used until an electronic
filing system is adopted for all documents. All files shall be saved to the Accela software: Street

Examples:

  • 4567 Any Street – Doe Inc. - CIT

  1. CIT – Citation
  2. COR – General Correspondence

2.3  Citizen and Staff Complaints
Purpose:
To provide guidance for how to respond to complaints received from citizens, other agencies or staff.
Policy and Procedures:
Complaints from the public are received via the website, the GoGov Application, by e-mail, by phone call
to report a violation, or by a letter to staff. Complaints from staff typically originate from observed
violations while out in the field.

There are two methods of achieving the Division’s goal of voluntary compliance and enforcement of all
applicable laws, codes, standards and regulations. The methods are (1) reactive, such as responding to
complaints and issuing citations; and (2) proactive, such as notifying interested parties of problems on the
property and investigating independently observed violations.

Complainant identity shall be considered confidential information not subject to disclosure. Code
Enforcement Officers shall not release the name of the source. If a Public Records Act request for Code
Enforcement materials is submitted, the officer shall immediately and directly report this to the Supervisor
and to the City Attorney’s Office.

 Allegations of violations from anonymous persons (which include both those persons who fail to provide
contact information to Code Enforcement as well as those who provide contact information but ask to
remain anonymous) may be investigated at the Division Manager’s discretion. If the Manager authorizes
an investigation to occur, and no violation can be independently determined by the Enforcement Officer,
the case may be closed. In order for an apparent violation that was witnessed solely by a complainant to
move forward to the enforcement stage, the complainant shall be agreeable to providing testimony (at an
administrative hearing, court proceeding, and/or via a declaration signed under penalty of perjury) if
necessary. This requirement is in addition to Code Enforcement’s request of additional information from
the complainant party substantiating their allegations.

2.4  Initial Steps, Investigation, and Informal Efforts to Obtain Voluntary Compliance and
Correction of Violations
Purpose:
To provide a consistent process for the Code Enforcement Division related to obtaining voluntary
compliance.
Policy and Procedures:
Upon receipt of a complaint or discovery of an actual violation, Department staff shall follow these actions:
  1. The Code Officer shall enter the information into the case tracking software and create a Code
  Enforcement file.
  2. The Code Enforcement Manager shall assign the file to an Enforcement Officer.
  3. The Enforcement Officer shall initiate an investigation and conduct research to determine if a
  violation(s) exists. Research may include internet searches.
  4. If during the investigation of a complaint it is unclear if a violation exists, Code Enforcement
  Officers may make contact with the owner of the property and/or other person(s) to gather
  additional evidence. A phone conversation may clear the property owner/tenant of any
  wrongdoing, or may give clarity of the facts of a potential violation. If communication by phone
  proves not to be feasible, and an initial drive-by site inspection does not garner the needed facts,
  then contact shall be made by mail.
  5. In all cases in which a violation exists, the Enforcement Officer shall provide the owner(s) and/or
  any other person(s) responsible for violations with a letter, which provides a summary and
  description of the apparent code violation and the City’s remedies and courses of action that may
  be pursued.
  6. If Voluntary Compliance is agreed upon, Code Enforcement Officers shall confirm in writing
  with the property owner/person responsible as to the required compliance course of action.
  Officers should allow a reasonable amount of time and opportunity for correction of the violations
  before the formal enforcement steps. While the amount of time allowed for compliance may vary,
  depending on the circumstances, those circumstances should be well-documented in writing to
  justify the period of time allowed for compliance or cure.
2.5  Requests for Extension
Purpose:

 To provide procedures for uniformly handling case files to provide consistent treatment of citizens related
to extension requests.
Policy and Procedures:
Any request for an extension of time to bring the property into compliance shall be provided on a letter
titled, “Request for Extension.” The letter shall be provided by the property owner. If approved – which
is at sole discretion of the assigned Enforcement Officer – the assigned Enforcement Officer shall initial
the letter and note the extension in the case file.
The Enforcement Officer shall subsequently mail a letter to the property owner/ responsible party
confirming the extension and advising them of the new compliance date. The complainant shall be
contacted and updated on the case status. Extensions may be granted for a reasonable period of time
depending on the circumstances, the stated reasons for the extension, and the nature of the violation. As
with other specified deadlines, the circumstances and reasoning for the length of the extension will be
well documented in the file. The extension will be granted for no more than 30 calendar days unless
circumstances clearly warrant a longer extension. In no event should the deadline for compliance be
extended for more than 90 calendar days. Authorization for any extension longer than 30 calendar days
must be obtained from the Code Enforcement Manager.
2.6  Scope of Inspection and Expectation of Privacy
Purpose:
To provide general guidelines for entry onto private property in the course of investigating reported or
observed violations. San Marino recognizes that entry onto private property for enforcement purposes is
governed by State law, constitutional considerations, and other applicable law.
Policy and Procedures:
Property owners have a right to privacy and are entitled to be free of illegal searches. If a property owner
has erected a 6-foot high or taller solid fence such as a chain link fence with slats, block fence, or wooden
fence around the rear yard of the property, the property owner has a reasonable expectation of privacy.
No Enforcement Officer shall use any artificial means to improve their position in an attempt to look over
a solid fence to view a violation, such as standing in the bed of a truck or climbing on top of an electrical

 Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
 Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government

BACKGROUND

The City has roughly 83 part-time positions that are filled by 47 employees (employees often fill
multiple positions). Part-time employees account for approximately one third of City staff. The
employees in many of these part-time positions provide direct services to our residents. For
instance, part-time Library staff provide necessary assistance with keeping the Library organized
and maintained, as well as, provide vital customer service assistance to patrons. Another large
portion of our part-time positions can be found in the Recreation Department. These part-time
employees organize many community events and student activities, and have been instrumental
in providing needed support to the community during the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore,
part-time employees provide various support in our Police Department, City Manager’s Office,
Parks & Public Works Department, and Community Development Department.

On December 9, 2015, the City Council, which did not include any of its current members,
approved Resolution No. R-15-21, increasing the rates of part-time classifications in order to
avoid compaction issues due to increases in the minimum wage that would occur in 2016. On
April 4, 2016, Senate Bill No. 3 (SB3) was signed by Governor Jerry Brown to increase the
minimum wage rate in California. Under SB3, the minimum wage increases incrementally until
2022, at which time the minimum wage will be adjusted annually per the annual Consumer Price
Index with a capitated rate (i.e. highest rate allowed) of 3.5 percent. The schedule for California’s
minimum wage until that point is as follows:

In the subsequent five years following approval of Resolution No. R-15-21, the City’s practice has
been to only make increases in the part-time salary schedule that were directly impacted by the
mandated minimum wage increases. As was stated in the December 11, 2019 staff report
amending the Part-time Salary Schedule, “Staff is looking into a long-term solution to address
these mandates, to provide a competitive salary for recruitment and retention purposes, and to
avoid salary compression issues.” (Salary compression, also known as “compaction,” is a
condition where classifications do not earn enough, or less, in comparison to subordinate
classifications within the same classification series.) In addition to this problem, we have several
other classification in other series which are not making competitive compensation in comparison
to classification in similar comparable agencies.

Continuation of this practice is no longer sustainable, as the rise of minimum wage
is causing compaction, and many of the part-time salaries are no longer as
competitive as comparable agencies. Therefore, staff conducted a salary study on the City’s
part-time positions to determine the effects of the minimum wage increase, and to ensure
competitive wages for the City’s part-time positions.

DISCUSSION

There are currently four classifications (approximately 31 positions) on the current salary range
that make below the new $14.00 minimum wage rate. This group includes Library Clerk, Library
Page, Park Attendant, and Recreation Program Leader.

There are currently seven classifications (approximately 40 positions) that are impacted by
compaction issues. This group includes Child Development Specialist, Library Assistant, Library
Monitor, Recreation Specialist, Maintenance Assistant, Police Cadet, and Professional Intern. For
these classes, a salary study was conducted.

Most of the part-time positions in the City are in classifications that do not have a full-time
equivalent position. There are, however, some part-time positions that are in classification that
have full-time equivalent positions that are paid in accordance to the San Marino City Employees
Association (SMCEA) Salary Schedule. During the salary study, it was found that there were part-
time classifications that were not making the same rate as their full-time counterpart. In some
cases (Code Enforcement Officer and Librarian II), it was found that the part-time positions were
paid lower than their full-time counterpart. In the case of Librarian I, it was found that two of

 the part-time positions, going back to 2014, made more than their full-time counterpart. Looking
through the files, staff could not determine the rationale for why the part-time salary rate for
Librarian I was higher than that of the salary rate for a full-time Librarian I.

A concern with having part-time staff in the same classification as their full-time counterpart, but
paid on different salary schedules is the principle of equal pay for work of equal value. This
principle is often adopted by agencies to ensure that consistent compensation decisions are made
in order to avoid illegal discrimination claims.

Another issue of concern with the City’s practice of having a separate Part-time Salary Schedule,
is that if and when the City wanted to hire a part-time employee for a position that is not
represented on the published Part-time Salary Schedule, staff would need to bring this to Council
as a separate item for approval. This would be especially problematic for higher-level
management classifications, as the City Manager does not have authority to pay a prospective
employee a salary that has not been approved by the City Council. Consequently, this could
potentially add delays in hiring staff, which may lead to losing out on prospective talent and
decreased efficiency of service to the community, during a time when the City would need to
urgently fill a position.

The most efficient and effective solution to many of the stated issues above would be for the City
to adopt one salary schedule, consolidating both part-time and full-time positions. This would
align part-time positions with their full-time counterpart and would reduce inefficiencies that
come with having a separate Part-time Salary Schedule.

If City Council was to approve aligning part-time classifications to their full-time counterpart and
combine into one salary schedule, it would reduce the salary schedule of two incumbents in the
Library I classification as discussed earlier. One option for Council to rectify this would be to Y-
rate the incumbents. Y-rating freezes the dollar amount of salary until which time that the
incumbents’ salary falls within the salary range of the classification. If approved, the Y-rating
would conclude on July 1, 2021 when the part-time salaries of the two incumbents come into
alignment with the SMCEA salary range for the Library I classification.

  Engaged and Connected Residents

BACKGROUND

In April 2020, the City Council supported a re-envisioning proposal that shifted the City’s
recreational approach towards broader community building. With the understanding that
community engagement programs do not typically result in significant revenues, it was anticipated
that those expenses would be offset by the revenue generated by the complementary contract
classes programming. The proposal’s implementation was described as a three-year phased in
process that would eventually result in an increased number of community events, more engaging
and relevant class offerings, and nimble pop-up programming for teens and adults.

The approval offered by the City Council at the April 24, 2020 meeting occurred during the very
early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic before we had a good sense of the ways or the intensity
that it would impact our operations. Therefore, during the FY 2020-21 budget process, the City
Council issued very clear direction to the City Manager to carefully monitor the impacts of the
novel coronavirus on revenues and programming for community services operations and return
if/when changes needed to be made or considered.

As a result, since the beginning of the fiscal year, City leadership has taken a very conservative
approach to expenditures. This practice reflects constant monitoring of the health crisis and its
potential impact on the City’s revenue sources.

Now in its tenth month of health order restrictions, the pandemic continues as reported
coronavirus cases, hospitalizations, and deaths increase at record numbers. Evolving health
orders, community fears, public optics, and a shared responsibility to safeguard residents has

Page 45 of 54  3-1
 significantly limited the City’s ability to provide and grow community programming and/or
accomplish many of the programming initiatives identified for Year One of the re-envisioning
proposal.

The Recreation Division has been severely affected operationally and fiscally. Over the past six
months, public health orders and community stewardship have restricted or eliminated the ability
to provide the programming we all envisioned in April of 2020. Given current circumstances, we
anticipate that public health orders will likely restrict community programming options through
summer, at a minimum. This holds especially true for contract (fee) classes, which generate the
bulk of the division's revenue. We should note that this trend is not unique to San Marino; municipalities
nationwide are grappling with similar challenges.

At 50% of the way through the fiscal year, the division's expenditures are less than 25% of
budgeted benchmarks and revenues are at 5%. The FY2020-21 operating budget authorized a
net cost for the Recreation Division of approximately $419,000 by the General Fund. If we
continue our current expenditure and revenue trends, the department will likely incur a net cost
of approximately $800,000, or roughly $380,000 more than expected.

Currently and historically, the Recreation Division has been the only operating unit with a
revenue-generating mandate. As a result, although the Finance Director is confident that other
savings in the operating budget will offset this $380K amount, we believe it best to request that
the City Council affirm this path forward.

Given that we are at the midpoint of the fiscal year, the time is optimal to return, as promised,
to present alternatives to the City Council and request direction for the remainder of the fiscal
year.

DISCUSSION

The pandemic has affected all aspects of municipal life. The service of recreation has been turned
upside down across the country and here in San Marino. Safer-at-home orders have created
stress and isolation for many in our community. Frankly, the need for community engagement is
greater than ever. As the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) continues to limit
physical interactions, as children remain in remote learning, and as employees continue
teleworking, social isolation continues to undoubtedly grow.

Although the health crisis has severely limited our “normal” programming, it does offer
opportunities for increased community engagement, albeit delivered in a different way. These
possibilities align with the City’s organizational priorities to further public visibility and dialogue.
They also create a means to provide a healthier, happier, and more connected San Marino. We
have also seen great success this year with our re-imagined programs, especially the Veterans’
Day exhibit and the Holiday Poinsettia gift baskets.

Given how well the community is responding to our new programming, engagement, and
outreach, we recommend continuing forward. If affirmed by the City Council, we will build upon
our previous successes to continue a series of engagement initiatives through June 30. Preliminary
ideas include activity kits, in-car and virtual programming options, and a limited offering of
allowable in-person events whenever possible and appropriate. A concerted effort will ensure

 that the proposal considers all age cohorts (children, young adults, adults, and older adults),
achieves variety in our targeted populations, and augments Crowell Public Library’s planned
community programming.

This is staff’s recommendation. However, if the City Council prefers to increase revenues or
decrease expenditures even further than we have already done, there are two alternative options,
neither of which are recommended by staff.

Alternative 1 – Reduce Personnel Costs (Not Recommended)

The bulk of the operational expenses in any department is staff costs; Community Services is no
different. We have already seen a significant reduction in personnel costs as a result of employees
electing to stay home during the pandemic. However, if the Council wants to further reduce
that number, lay-offs would be necessary.

The City’s commitment from the beginning has been to “keep our employees whole,” to the best
of our ability. Moving to lay-offs sends a very different message and will impact morale at a time
when we are already challenged in that area. Further, all of our working employees are
performing critical community functions, including programming and staffing the EOC Resident
Hotline.

Alternative 2 – Incorporate Cost Recovery into Community Programming (Not Recommended)

The only way to increase our revenues during the pandemic is to charge more for what we are
offering. This would essentially mean charging residents for participating in our community
engagement activities (i.e. charging people to view the Veterans’ Day exhibit, receiving the holiday
gifts, etc.).

However, recreation-based cost recovery is about supply and demand, both of which are
currently restricted by public health orders and personal choices. Even if the City moves forward
with this approach, a high level of success is improbable. There are many factors outside the
City’s control to consider, including contractor and vendor availability, health protocols,
participant willingness, impact to the community’s perception of the City, etc. Cost recovery for
virtual programming is also not viable. While there could be potential for a few successful
offerings, local and national trends show a marked decrease in demand for this type of format. It
is unlikely that community members will want to pay a fee for virtual programming.

FISCAL IMPACT & PROCUREMENT REVIEW

Staff recommends that we continue with our current programming to build community
engagement and morale, while being mindful of maintaining conservative expenditures. As noted
above, the Finance Director anticipates that this will result in approximately an additional
$380,000 that will need to be absorbed by the operating budget. Again, as noted above, the
Finance Director is confident, based on existing citywide revenue and expenditure trends, that
no additional appropriation of funds is necessary to accommodate this community programming
philosophy.

BACKGROUND

During the Fiscal Year 2019-20 budget process, staff worked together with the City Council
Budget Liaisons (then Council Members Jakubowski and Ude) to develop an innovative and
streamlined budget process that ultimately led to a successful adoption of the budget on May 31,
2019. The FY 2020-21 budget process followed a similar process, and the budget was successfully
adopted on June 26, 2020.

One prominent element of both prior budget cycles was the brainstorming and selection of
priority initiatives. Priority initiatives were defined as one-time, special projects that were
additions to the regular day-to-day operational tasks and functions of each department. The
intention of priority initiatives was to allow City Council (with feedback from the community and
staff) to set the workplan of each department for the year.

City Council approved 5 priority initiatives for FY 2020-21. They are as follows:

  1. Renovate the San Marino Center into a state-of-the art Community Center
  2. Launch a robust Chinese translation and engagement program to ensure all residents have
  access to critical information and services

  4. Beautify Huntington Drive and medians to make the area more business-friendly and
  attractive using signage and landscaping
  5. Create a traffic safety program, including a motorcycle enforcement and investigation

A mid-year status update on these priority initiatives is included here as Attachment 1.

While the priority initiative selection process was especially helpful in FY 2019-2020, when staff
made a commitment to bring no additional costs outside of approved priority initiatives, we saw
last year that we may have outgrown the need for this process. Three main issues arose during
the priority initiative selection process and the subsequent months:

    It became difficult to differentiate what was a priority initiative and what was purely a
  process improvement or operational goal. While we attempted to define priority
  initiatives as significant policy shifts or significant monetary investments, there was still a
  bit of a gray area in terms of what should truly be a priority initiative and what should be
  proposed during the operational or Capital Improvement Project (CIP) budgets.

    The priority initiative process gave Council three opportunities to discuss and move
  forward priority initiatives: at the first initial brainstorming session, after staff brought back
  more detailed information about budget and feasibility, and lastly during the actual budget
  adoption. In a year where staff has been directed to look for efficiencies, we have realized
  that takes significant time and attention from both staff and Council. We believe we can
  streamline this process without sacrificing meaningful discussions.

    Most importantly, we came to see that approved priority initiatives and the regular day-
  to-day operations did not actually represent each department’s complete workplan for
  the year. Many departments did not have an official priority initiative assigned to them,
  but still had special projects they were working on outside of their daily operations.
  Others had new projects assigned to them throughout the year, as issues arose. Because
  staff had no overarching document to help Council understand the impact any new project
  would have on their other priorities for the year, workloads in some departments became
  unmanageable.

Because of this, staff had discussions with the Budget Liaisons (Mayor Ude and Vice Mayor
Jakubowski) and decided to retire the priority initiative process and replace it with a more flexible
goal-setting session and the development of true department workplans. The new process is
described below in more detail, but the ultimate goal will be to create and approve true workplans
for each department so that expectations for the year are set up front. This will hopefully set the
foundation for more effective dialogue about the impact on approved workplans as new projects
arise throughout the year.

Today’s meeting marks the kickoff of the FY 2021-22 budget process, and the budget calendar is
attached to this staff report as Attachment 2. The calendar follows a similar timeline and structure
as last year’s budget process, with a few key changes: 1) the removal of the priority initiative
process and replacement with today’s goal-setting session, and 2) the breakout of the CIP
presentation into two separate meetings – one for equipment, and one for infrastructure.

Today’s goal-setting session will be free-form and discussion based, using the City’s approved
Critical Success Factors as our guide posts. As a reminder, our eight Critical Success Factors are
as follows:

    Engaged and Connected Residents
    Efficient, Responsive, and Effective City Services
    Safe Community
    Well-Maintained Infrastructure
    Fiscally Responsible and Transparent City Government
    Attractive, Complementary Business District
    Inviting and Relevant City Facilities
    Beautiful, Preserved, Single-Family Neighborhoods

The purpose of this brainstorming session will be to give staff suggestions and ideas related to
your overall goals and priorities for the next year – whether they have budget impacts or not.
And instead of only focusing on issues “big” enough to be priority initiatives, we are asking you
to give us your insights into anything – whether its big or small, a cost savings idea or a large
budget item.

In non-COVID-times, we would have large easels to display each idea you give us, but because of
safety protocols, staff will be taking written notes. While staff will be available to answer questions
and give any contextual understanding necessary, staff will not advocate for or petition against
any proposal. We are purely interested in understanding Council’s desires for the next year so
we can take this into account when proposing our workplans and budgets for next fiscal year.

After today’s meeting, staff will engage with the community and get their thoughts on what they
would like to see the City focus on next year. In the past, we have asked the community to weigh
in on potential priority initiatives already proposed by Council, but this year, we will be asking
them to give us their own ideas that we can consider alongside of yours. We will do this through
a virtual town hall on February 1st at 6:00pm, and an online community survey that will be live
throughout the month of February.

Please note that this is one major change from last year to streamline the process and make it

We know that, like any new process, there may be some kinks that need to be worked as we go
along, and potentially refined again for the following year’s budget. We hope, however, that it
sets us up for more holistic departmental budget presentations that shows you the true proposed
workplan of each department, including both special projects, new efficiencies, and their day-to-
day operating needs. This will allow for staff and Council to have more effective and transparent
conversations about the impact on a department’s workplan as new priorities arise throughout
the year and limit the addition of new special projects to those that are truly important to take
on.
